extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers or fans of comedy history and biographies
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biography of Douglas Kenney covering his life, career (National Lampoon, Animal House, Caddyshack), comedic style, and legacy. Not an instructional rubric but contains descriptive statements about comedic style and techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: New wave comedy style (National Lampoon)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dark, irreverent style of humor described as the 'new wave' of comedy during the 1970s: 'slash-and-burn stuff that alternated in pitch but moved very much on the offensive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics and examples from the page: 'disrespect everything, mostly yourself' (a sort of reverse deism); roots in W.A.S.P. and Irish Catholic culture with a Canadian detachment; 'alienation is funny' — mixing existentialist sensibility with lowbrow elements (Kenney: 'if you take an existentialist, add a hot Camaro, a skateboard, and a lot of dope, you have a working, vital existentialist'). Use offensiveness, self-deprecation, and cultural detachment as tools to produce this tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody via faux-diary (example: 'Mrs. Agnew's Diary')
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a first-person faux-diary column to satirize public figures and politics (the Lampoon ran 'Mrs. Agnew's Diary', purporting to be the diary of Spiro Agnew's wife).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: adopt a consistent diarist voice representing a well-known figure (or relation) to lampoon politicians and events; modelled on Private Eye's 'Mrs. Wilson's Diary' — Americanize the comedic viewpoint and maintain recurring installments. Example on page: 'Mrs. Agnew's Diary' chronicled life as Second Lady with 'Spiggy', Richard Nixon, and other famous politicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format parody (example: High School Yearbook Parody)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodying a specific publication format (e.g., a high school yearbook) to create satirical content — the National Lampoon 1964 High School Yearbook Parody is cited as the magazine's best-selling edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach: faithfully mimic the conventions and tropes of the target format (layout, captions, types of entries) while subverting content for comedic effect. The page notes the yearbook parody was based on an earlier two-page piece and used collaborative writing (Kenney with P. J. O'Rourke and an earlier idea with Michael O'Donoghue) — implies iterative development from smaller bits to a full-format parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative magazine comedy production model
rubrics_metrics.description: National Lampoon's comedic output arose from a recurring group and editorial structure (Kenney: a group of about 30 people worked repeatedly together; roles included editor-in-chief, senior editor, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production guidance implied by the page: rely on a stable, recurring ensemble of writers and editors; editorial leadership shapes voice and direction; allow contributors freedom (Kenney sometimes took extended breaks) while maintaining regular features (e.g., recurring columns always submitted). Business arrangements (e.g., buyout contracts) and editorial roles influenced the magazine's operation and longevity.
